topics.title: Amazon VPC and public vs private subnets

kcs.statement: A VPC is a logically isolated virtual network in one AWS Region, defined by an IP address range (a CIDR block), that can span all Availability Zones in that Region.
Each subnet lives in exactly one Availability Zone, so a highly available design places subnets in at least two AZs.
A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway; a private subnet has no direct route to the internet, so back-end resources such as databases are placed there.

serves.reason: VPC and subnet roles are the base vocabulary for every networking service question on the exam

requires.reason: A subnet is defined as living in one AZ; the KC cannot be checked without knowing what an AZ is

topics.title: Internet gateways, NAT gateways and route tables

kcs.statement: An internet gateway attaches to a VPC and allows two-way traffic between the internet and resources with public IP addresses in public subnets.

A NAT gateway, placed in a public subnet, lets instances in private subnets start outbound internet connections (for example, to download patches) while blocking connections initiated from the internet.

A subnet's route table decides where its traffic goes: a default route to an internet gateway makes the subnet public, while a default route to a NAT gateway keeps it private with outbound-only access.

requires.reason: The gateway roles are defined in terms of public and private subnets

topics.title: Security groups vs network ACLs

kcs.statement: A security group is a stateful firewall attached to an instance's network interface: it has allow rules only, and return traffic for an allowed request is permitted automatically.
A network ACL is a stateless firewall at the subnet boundary: it has numbered allow and deny rules evaluated lowest number first, and return traffic must be explicitly allowed.
A new security group denies all inbound and allows all outbound traffic, while a VPC's default network ACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic.
To block one specific IP address or range, add a deny rule to a network ACL, because security groups cannot express deny rules.

serves.reason: The exam names VPC security (security groups, network ACLs) explicitly and asks which one fits a stated need

requires.reason: Network ACLs are defined as acting at the subnet boundary

kcs.statement: VPC Flow Logs record metadata about IP traffic to and from network interfaces in a VPC (source, destination, port, accepted or rejected), for troubleshooting connectivity and security analysis; they do not capture packet contents.

topics.title: VPC peering, VPC endpoints and PrivateLink

kcs.statement: VPC peering privately connects two VPCs, even across accounts or Regions, so they route traffic as one network; peering is not transitive and the two CIDR ranges must not overlap.
A VPC endpoint lets resources in a private subnet reach AWS services such as S3 without going over the internet, an internet gateway or a NAT gateway.
Gateway endpoints serve only S3 and DynamoDB; interface endpoints, powered by AWS PrivateLink, expose other AWS services or a third party's service privately inside your VPC.

serves.reason: Exam items ask how to reach S3 privately or connect two VPCs; these are the answers

topics.title: AWS VPN: Site-to-Site and Client VPN

kcs.statement: AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates an encrypted IPsec connection over the public internet between an on-premises network and a VPC; it can be set up quickly, but bandwidth and latency vary with internet conditions.
AWS Client VPN connects individual users' devices, such as remote employees' laptops, to AWS or on-premises networks, whereas Site-to-Site VPN joins whole networks.

serves.reason: The exam guide lists AWS VPN among network connectivity options to choose between

requires.reason: The VPN's AWS end is a VPC, which must already be defined

topics.title: AWS Direct Connect: a private line to AWS

kcs.statement: AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated private network connection from an on-premises data center to AWS that bypasses the public internet, giving consistent bandwidth and latency.
A new Direct Connect connection takes weeks to provision, so a requirement for connectivity within days points to Site-to-Site VPN instead.
Direct Connect traffic is private but not encrypted by default; running a Site-to-Site VPN over it adds IPsec encryption, and a VPN can also serve as a lower-cost backup link.

serves.reason: Direct Connect is named in the exam guide's connectivity options and a frequent distractor against VPN

requires.reason: The lead-time and encryption KCs are stated as contrasts with Site-to-Site VPN

topics.title: Transit Gateway: one hub for many networks

kcs.statement: AWS Transit Gateway is a regional hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks (through VPN or Direct Connect) via one gateway, in a hub-and-spoke design.
Fully meshing n VPCs with peering needs n(n−1)/2 connections because peering is not transitive, so Transit Gateway is the choice when many VPCs must all reach each other.

serves.reason: Transit Gateway appears in the exam's networking service list as the answer for many-VPC connectivity

requires.reason: The choice is stated as a contrast with non-transitive peering

topics.title: Amazon Route 53: DNS, domains and health checks

kcs.statement: Amazon Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service: it translates domain names into IP addresses and can also register domain names.
A hosted zone holds the DNS records for one domain; a public hosted zone answers queries from the internet and a private hosted zone answers only inside associated VPCs.
Route 53 health checks monitor endpoints so that DNS stops returning an unhealthy endpoint and sends users to a healthy one.

serves.reason: The exam guide asks learners to understand the purpose of Route 53

topics.title: Route 53 routing policies

kcs.statement: Simple routing returns one record for a name, while weighted routing splits traffic between records by assigned weights, for example 90/10 to test a new version.
Latency-based routing sends each user to the AWS Region that gives that user the lowest network latency.
Failover routing sends traffic to a primary resource while its health check passes and to a secondary resource when it fails, supporting active-passive disaster recovery.
Geolocation routing picks the record by the user's country or continent, for localized content or legal restrictions, regardless of which Region would be fastest.

topics.title: Amazon CloudFront: caching content at the edge

kcs.statement: Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network that caches copies of content at edge locations, so users get lower latency than fetching from the origin Region.
A CloudFront distribution fetches content from an origin such as an S3 bucket, a load balancer or an EC2 instance, and serves cached copies until they expire or are invalidated.
CloudFront reduces load on the origin because cached requests never reach it, and AWS Shield Standard DDoS protection applies to CloudFront at no extra cost.

topics.title: Global Accelerator vs CloudFront

kcs.statement: AWS Global Accelerator gives an application two static anycast IP addresses and carries user traffic from the nearest edge location over the AWS global network, improving latency and availability.

Global Accelerator does not cache content: choose CloudFront for cacheable web content and Global Accelerator for non-HTTP traffic such as UDP gaming or when clients need fixed IP addresses with fast regional failover.

topics.title: Relational vs NoSQL databases

kcs.statement: A relational database stores data in tables with a fixed schema, links rows by keys and is queried with SQL, supporting joins and multi-row transactions.
NoSQL databases (key-value, document, graph, in-memory) use flexible schemas and scale horizontally, giving up complex joins in exchange for speed at very large scale.

serves.reason: Every database selection question starts by placing the requirement on the relational or NoSQL side

topics.title: Managed databases vs databases on EC2

kcs.statement: With a managed database such as RDS, AWS handles provisioning, OS and engine patching, automated backups and hardware failure, while the customer manages schemas, data, user access and network settings.
Run a database on EC2 only when you need OS-level access, an engine or version the managed services do not offer, or full configuration control; you then own patching, backups and high availability.

topics.title: Amazon RDS: Multi-AZ, read replicas and backups

kcs.statement: Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service supporting the MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, Db2 and Aurora engines.
In an RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, a synchronous standby in a second AZ takes over automatically on failure; its purpose is availability, not extra read capacity.
RDS read replicas are asynchronous copies, in the same or another Region, that serve read-only queries to scale read-heavy workloads.
RDS automated backups allow point-in-time restore within a retention period of up to 35 days, while manual snapshots are kept until you delete them.

serves.reason: RDS is the exam's default relational database answer and its HA options are frequently tested

topics.title: Amazon Aurora: AWS-built relational engine

kcs.statement: Amazon Aurora is an AWS-built relational engine, compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL and managed through RDS, that AWS rates at up to 5× MySQL and 3× PostgreSQL throughput.
Aurora keeps six copies of data across three AZs with storage that grows automatically, and Aurora Serverless scales capacity automatically for variable or unpredictable workloads.

serves.reason: Aurora is the exam answer for high-performance, highly available MySQL/PostgreSQL

requires.reason: Aurora is defined as an RDS engine and compared with standard RDS

topics.title: Amazon DynamoDB: serverless NoSQL at any scale

kcs.statement: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL key-value and document database delivering single-digit-millisecond performance at any scale.
DynamoDB stores items made of attributes in tables; each item is identified by a primary key (a partition key, optionally with a sort key), and items in one table may have different attributes.
DynamoDB on-demand capacity charges per request and suits unpredictable traffic, while provisioned capacity sets read and write capacity in advance and suits steady, predictable traffic.
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache that cuts DynamoDB reads to microseconds, and global tables replicate a table across Regions with writes accepted in every Region.

serves.reason: DynamoDB is the exam's default NoSQL answer and appears in many scenarios

requires.reason: DynamoDB is placed in the NoSQL family defined there

topics.title: Amazon ElastiCache: in-memory caching

kcs.statement: Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory data store compatible with Redis OSS, Valkey and Memcached, giving sub-millisecond reads and offloading repeated queries from a database.
Typical ElastiCache uses are caching frequent database query results and storing user session data; adding a cache usually requires application code changes.
DAX caches only DynamoDB tables, so a cache in front of RDS, Aurora or another data source calls for ElastiCache rather than DAX.

serves.reason: The exam guide names ElastiCache as the memory-based database to identify

requires.reason: ElastiCache is placed as the in-memory member of the NoSQL family

topics.title: DocumentDB and Neptune: document and graph data

kcs.statement: Amazon DocumentDB is a managed document database with MongoDB compatibility, chosen to run MongoDB-style JSON document workloads as a managed service.
Amazon Neptune is a managed graph database for highly connected data such as social networks, recommendation engines and fraud-detection relationships.

topics.title: Choosing a database service for a requirement

kcs.statement: Map requirement cues to services: SQL with joins → RDS; MySQL/PostgreSQL needing top performance and availability → Aurora; key-value at massive scale → DynamoDB; sub-millisecond caching → ElastiCache; MongoDB → DocumentDB; relationship graphs → Neptune.
For database availability choose RDS Multi-AZ, for read-heavy scaling choose read replicas or a cache, and for low-latency writes in several Regions choose DynamoDB global tables.
